label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, pool-exhaustion, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 8 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Code planned the action its diagnosis named (redeploy payments-api: PROVIDER_BREAKER on (unchanged), CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT cents (unchanged), REFUND_CONNECTION kept -> returned); in an evaluation run nobody is asked, and nothing ran. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing (klaxon.faults).

case.name: pool-exhaustion
case.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500.
case.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

fault.name: pool-exhaustion
fault.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
fault.cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500
expected_symptoms: the pool runs dry about 40 to 50 s after the deploy; then POST /payments takes 5 to 8 s (a worker thread, then the pool's 5 s wait) and fails with a 500: the p95 latency passes 7 s, and the 5xx share passes 70% within a minute
the payments API logs 'unhandled error' with PoolTimeout: no connection within 5 s
its health check fails too, so docker marks it unhealthy, while PostgreSQL itself is up
the traffic's clients retry and give up: many payments end with their outcome unknown, and arrivals past 64 in flight are shed
the money check passes: a payment that never got a connection was never charged, and one charged before its answer was lost is confirmed by its webhook
fault.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

alert.summary: Payments are failing: over the last minute, 87% of the answers to POST /payments on payments-api were 5xx (4.48 per second), above the threshold of 20%. Payments are slow: over the last minute, the p95 latency of POST /payments on payments-api was 7.4 s, above the threshold of 2 s.

diagnosis.hypothesis: payments-api was redeployed at 08:04:10 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. The most likely effect is that each refund request keeps its PostgreSQL pool connection after it finishes instead of returning it. Refunds still succeed quickly (9-25 ms), so the leak is silent at first. After about a minute, enough refunds have run to drain the psycopg pool. From then on, every request that needs a database connection, on both POST /payments and POST /payments/{id}/refunds, waits for the pool timeout (about 5-7 s). It then fails with PoolTimeout and returns 500. This explains both alert conditions: 87% 5xx and a p95 of 7.4 s. The provider is not involved, since its calls stay at about 5 ms. What the evidence leaves open: I did not see pool-occupancy metrics or code, so the leak itself is inferred from the setting's name and the timing, not observed. I also did not confirm what REFUND_CONNECTION was set to before this deploy.

evidence.shows: 5xx on /payments appear only from 08:05:20, reaching 4.8/s. 201s fall at the same time. Before that, responses were healthy.
payments-api was the only service changed recently: redeployed at 08:04:10 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. Everything else was created at 08:02:44.
The 500s on POST /payments are psycopg_pool PoolTimeout exceptions, so the database connection pool is exhausted.
p95 latency of both /payments and /refunds jumps from about 30 ms to about 7.1-7.4 s at 08:05:20, a uniform wait consistent with a pool timeout.

arguments.query: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, http_request_method, url_template, server_address) (rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service_name="payments-api"}[1m])))

evidence.shows: Calls from payments-api to fake-provider stay at about 5 ms p95 throughout, so slow provider calls are not what holds connections.
A failing POST /payments trace spends about 6.5 s with no database or provider span, only Redis calls, and ends in PoolTimeout. The time goes to waiting for a pool connection.

Refunds after the deploy (08:04:18-08:04:50) completed successfully in 9-25 ms. Connections were exhausted roughly a minute later, consistent with each finished refund leaking a connection rather than holding it during slow work.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to its settings from before the 08:04:10 deploy, presumably the setting where refunds release their DB connection. Recreating the container also resets the exhausted pool. Then confirm that the 5xx rate and p95 on POST /payments return to normal, and run money_check. Requests that failed with 500 during the incident should be safe for clients to retry with their idempotency keys; verify that no payment was left half-recorded. Follow up by fixing or removing the REFUND_CONNECTION=kept path in code.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api restarts, so payment and refund requests pause or fail briefly during the restart, adding to failures that are already happening. If the previous setting also had a problem, the rollback would bring it back. In-flight requests that are cut off may leave a provider charge without a recorded response, but idempotency keys and webhooks should reconcile it. The rollback does not repair any money already booked wrong.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: Redeploy payments-api with the current settings (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents) on image sha256:208369178c56. This would bring the leak back, so do it only if the rollback causes a worse, different failure.
